trial_name: LOVIT — Intravenous Vitamin C in Adults with Sepsis in the Intensive Care Unit (2022)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Lamontagne F, Masse MH, Menard J, Sprague S, Pinto R, Heyland DK, et al. Intravenous Vitamin C in Adults with Sepsis in the Intensive Care Unit. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(25):2387-2398.
one_liner: High-dose intravenous vitamin C in ICU adults with sepsis receiving vasopressors increased the 28-day composite risk of death or persistent organ dysfunction.

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) admitted to ICU for ≤24 hours with suspected or confirmed infection receiving vasopressors.
pico.intervention: Intravenous vitamin C (ascorbic acid) 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for up to 96 hours (maximum 16 doses).
pico.comparison: Matching placebo intravenous infusion every 6 hours for up to 96 hours alongside usual care.
pico.outcome: Composite of death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28.

background.existing_knowledge: Critically ill patients with sepsis frequently have low circulating vitamin C levels due to increased consumption, reduced intake/absorption, and altered distribution. Vitamin C has antioxidant, endothelial-stabilising, and cofactor roles in catecholamine synthesis and immune function.
background.knowledge_gap: Early small trials of vitamin C monotherapy or metabolic resuscitation produced heterogeneous signals for shock resolution and mortality, but were underpowered or relied on surrogate endpoints while off-label use grew.
background.hypothesis: A 96-hour course of high-dose IV vitamin C reduces death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28 compared with placebo in ICU adults with sepsis requiring vasopressors.

methods.design: Multicentre, international, investigator-initiated, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT.
methods.setting: 35 ICUs in Canada, France, and New Zealand; enrolled November 2018 to July 2021.

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) admitted to ICU for ≤24 hours
Suspected or confirmed infection as primary reason for ICU admission
exclusion: History of kidney stones within previous year
Limitations of life-sustaining treatment or expected death within 48 hours
Receipt of IV vitamin C during current hospitalisation (excluding parenteral nutrition)
Inability to obtain consent within local frameworks

methods.intervention: Intravenous vitamin C (ascorbic acid) 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for up to 96 hours (maximum 16 doses), initiated as soon as feasible.
methods.comparison: Matching placebo IV infusion every 6 hours for up to 96 hours plus usual sepsis care.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (participants, clinicians, investigators, and outcome assessors); pharmacy-dispensed identical study preparations.
methods.sample_size_power: 770 patients needed to detect a 10% absolute reduction in primary outcome (50% to 40%) with 80% power at 2-sided alpha 0.05; planned 800; 872 randomised; primary ITT analysis.
methods.primary_outcome: Composite of death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28 (defined as vasopressor requirement, invasive mechanical ventilation, or new renal-replacement therapy).
secondary_outcomes: Days without organ dysfunction in ICU to day 28
methods.follow_up: Primary endpoint at day 28; survival and quality of life assessed to 6 months.

headline_bullets: Primary composite outcome of death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28 was significantly higher in the vitamin C group (44.5% vs 38.5%; RR 1.21; P=0.01).
The primary endpoint signal was driven predominantly by increased 28-day mortality (35.4% vs 31.6%; RR 1.17).
No improvements were observed in organ support-free days, ventilator-free days, vasopressor-free days, or 6-month survival.

outcomes_table.outcome: Death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28 (primary)
outcomes_table.note: Persistent organ dysfunction defined as vasopressor use, invasive mechanical ventilation, or new RRT

outcomes_table.outcome: Days without organ dysfunction in ICU (to day 28)
outcomes_table.note: Higher values indicate more days alive and free of organ dysfunction
No difference in severe AKI rates

safety: Hypoglycaemia: 26/429 (6.1%) in vitamin C vs 22/433 (5.1%) in placebo (RR 1.25; 95% CI 0.73 to 2.14), influenced by glucose meter point-of-care interference artefact.
Adjudicated serious adverse events: 1/429 (0.2%) in vitamin C vs 0/433 (0%) in placebo, due to one life-threatening anaphylaxis event in the vitamin C group.
Stage 3 acute kidney injury occurred in 162/429 (37.8%) vs 164/433 (37.9%) (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.19).

domains.notes: Central randomisation with allocation concealment, stratified by trial site.
Double-blind using identical study preparations dispensed by pharmacy; low risk of co-intervention bias.
872 randomised; 8 ineligible excluded post-randomisation; 1 deferred-consent participant retained for primary outcome only; 1 missing day 28 status.
99.1% vs 98.6% received ≥1 infusion; median 16 doses (IQR 14-16) both groups; open-label exposure 0.2% in both arms.
Well balanced: age 65±14 vs 67±14; APACHE II 24±7 vs 24±7; SOFA 12±3 vs 12±3; invasive vent 48.7% vs 49.2%; corticosteroids 65.5% vs 60.7%; thiamine 26.1% vs 24.5%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong given double blinding, central randomisation, high protocol adherence, and balanced co-interventions.

domains.notes: Typical ICU septic shock population (older, high APACHE II/SOFA, ~50% ventilated); mostly enrolled in Canadian ICUs with contributions from France and New Zealand.
Directly applies to adult ICU patients with vasopressor-dependent sepsis in high-income settings; does not inform non-ICU sepsis, pediatrics, or alternative dosing schedules.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for adult ICU patients with vasopressor-dependent sepsis in similar health systems, but limited for non-ICU populations.

strengths: Large, international, multicentre, double-blind placebo-controlled design
High protocol adherence and minimal open-label vitamin C contamination
Patient-centred primary outcome with follow-up extending to 6 months
Balanced baseline characteristics and co-intervention delivery
limitations: Composite primary outcome driven by mortality while secondary components showed smaller non-significant differences
Prespecified adjusted analysis attenuated the effect estimate (RR 1.15; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.47)
Baseline vitamin C levels measured in a subset only (324 vs 322; mean 20.6±70.6 vs 19.1±39.7 µmol/L) with no post-treatment levels reported

critical_appraisal.summary: LOVIT is a rigorous, high-quality RCT providing definitive evidence that high-dose IV vitamin C does not improve outcomes in vasopressor-dependent ICU sepsis and carries potential harm.
strengths: Double-blind design with identical matching placebo
Excellent protocol compliance and low open-label contamination
weaknesses: Interpretive complexity of composite outcome driven by mortality component
Lack of systematic post-dose pharmacodynamic plasma vitamin C measurements

sections.authors_conclusion: In adults with sepsis receiving vasopressors in the ICU, those who received intravenous vitamin C had a higher risk of death or persistent organ dysfunction at 28 days than those who received placebo.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: High-dose IV vitamin C should not be routinely administered to adult ICU patients with sepsis requiring vasopressors.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with sepsis or septic shock requiring vasopressor support.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean nutritional replacement or lower-dose physiologic supplementation in proven deficiency is harmful.
implementation_caveats: High-dose IV vitamin C can cause point-of-care blood glucose meter interference, risking iatrogenic hypoglycemia or inappropriate insulin delivery
Cessation of routine off-label use should be reinforced in clinical guidelines

controversies.topic: Biological mechanism of harm vs pro-oxidant risk
controversies.notes: Critiques highlighted that high-dose vitamin C acts pharmacologically rather than nutritionally, with potential pro-oxidant chemistry in specific microenvironments.
A secondary analysis hypothesized that abrupt cessation after 96 hours might cause rebound withdrawal harm, though this remains unverified by PK data.
Bayesian reanalyses showed sensitivity to prior beliefs, but editorial consensus maintained that Bayesian models should not override robust frequentist harm signals.
LOVIT catalyzed rapid recommendation guidelines and Japanese guideline updates to advise against routine IV vitamin C in sepsis.

context_related_trials.relation: Multicentre follow-up trial of early vitamin C in sepsis/septic shock that similarly showed no clinically important benefit.

unresolved_questions: Whether lower physiological dosing or prolonged tapered regimens avoid abrupt withdrawal effects without toxicity
Whether targeted therapy based on baseline plasma vitamin C levels would yield different outcomes

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Do not give high-dose IV vitamin C in septic shock; LOVIT showed increased 28-day death or persistent organ dysfunction without organ support benefit.
